Q: Why is Spring Boot still used in large-scale systems despite newer backend frameworks? A:

You didn't mention Rust at all in your question, which makes me think your searches have been quite biased towards something you are not mentioning in your question.

Many enterprise applications still use it because you don't just rewrite applications which likely have dozens if not hundreds of man-years of development invested in them. The fact that a Go or a Rust comes into existence and some Stack Overflow survey says people like them does not immediately validate throwing away thousands, millions or billions of dollars to spend years rewriting the existing application and end up with exactly the same thing, but with a boatload of regression bugs added to it. That's just the way it is. If something is Java it will stay Java. If something is Spring, it will stay Spring.

The more relevant question would be: why use it for new applications? The answer is going to be equally uninspiring... companies will keep using it because that's what they know. Or rather - that's what the workforce knows. Java is a very mature platform, just like .NET is. Plenty of people that can be hired or contracted to do work and do it well and teach juniors to get to a higher skill level quicker.

Which I assume... is where your interest comes from, even though you're not specifically asking about it. Why would you learn Spring Boot? Because there is work. Not necessarily fun work. But the need to eat is more important than fun. You're not stuck with Java though; .NET is an equally viable option and might even be the better choice depending on what part of the world you live in. Rust is on a steady climb as well.

Q: How do I order documentation for package declarations in go A:

You can’t reliably control the order of package documentation across multiple files. While it may appear to follow file order, that behavior isn’t guaranteed.

The idiomatic approach is to define the package comment in a single place (usually doc.go) and avoid duplicating it in other files.

According to a comment from the Go docs (go.dev/doc/comment)

For multi-file packages, the package comment should only be in one source file. If multiple files have package comments, they are concatenated to form one large comment for the entire package.
